Hi! We're Alex & Victoria, a Danish couple in our thirties, travelling the world with our two young children. Learn more about us here.

main_topic.h_title: The capital of Northern Thailand
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: It’s hard to skip Chiang Mai when visiting the beautiful north of Thailand.
And it would be a real shame to miss this part of Thailand !
Beyond being a charming city with great food and literally hundreds (!) of temples, it also serves as the perfect base for exploring the nearby mountains, hill tribe villages and waterfalls.

We spent 10 nights in Chiang Mai at Yi’s Garden Villa (adlink), and while that’s more than enough for most, we could easily have stayed twice as long. The atmosphere is wonderful, and there’s just so much to do.
In this guide to where to stay in Chiang Mai, we share recommendations for some of the best hotels in Chiang Mai, from budget-friendly stays to great value mid-range hotels and luxurious options.
Hopefully, it helps you find the best place to stay in Chiang Mai for your trip, so you can make the most of your time in the city.

main_topic.h_title: Our favourites: The best hotels in Chiang Mai
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: Budget: Yi’s Garden Villa – We stayed here for 10 nights and loved it. A pool and comfortable rooms with air conditioning at a great price in the old town.
Value for money: The Inside House – Photogenic hotel in the old town with private pools at reasonable prices.
Luxury: 137 Pillars House – Elegant luxury hotel with a colonial-inspired design, just minutes from the eastern city gate.
Ultra-luxury: Four Seasons Resort Chiang Mai – One of Northern Thailand’s most luxurious resorts, set in stunning natural surroundings just 30 minutes from the city.

main_topic.h_title: Where is Chiang Mai?
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: Chiang Mai is the largest city in Northern Thailand, situated about 700 kilometres (435 miles) north of Bangkok.
The city sits 300 metres above sea level in a valley surrounded by mountains.
Chiang Mai is centred around the old town, which is encircled by a moat. Many of Chiang Mai’s most famous sights and things to do can be found here.

main_topic.h_title: How many days to spend in Chiang Mai
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: We spent nine full days in Chiang Mai (10 nights), going out to explore almost every day. With a nine-month-old baby in tow, we took things at a relaxed pace and avoided packing the days too tightly.
How long you should stay in Chiang Mai depends entirely on what you’re looking for.
If you’re also thinking about where to stay in Chiang Mai, the length of your trip might influence whether you pick a central hotel for easy sightseeing or a quieter guesthouse for a longer stay.
Some will find a few days enough to see the main sights, while others see it as an ideal place to settle for months – especially backpackers and digital nomads.

main_topic.h_title: Examples of how long to stay in Chiang Mai:
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: 1 full day: In just one day, you can stroll through the old town, visit several stunning temples and take in the charming atmosphere – but you’ll be missing out on a lot.
2-3 full days: If you only have two weeks to explore multiple parts of Thailand, you can still experience a lot in Chiang Mai with just two or three full, well-planned days.
4-5 full days: Four to five days will be a more relaxed pace for most people and allow for day trips beyond the city centre.
1 week: With a week in Chiang Mai, you can explore at a relaxed pace, visit some lesser-known things to do and even take a trip to Chiang Rai or Pai.

main_topic.h_title: Where to stay in Chiang Mai
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: Chiang Mai has long been a popular destination for backpackers and those looking to experience Northern Thailand on a budget, and there are many best budget hotels in Chiang Mai to choose from.
Beyond that, there’s no shortage of hotel beds – with everything from lovely boutique hotels to five-star luxury.
You’ll also find modern apartments in complexes with pools and gyms (something digital nomads often appreciate) as well as homestays tucked away in quiet mountain villages.
No matter the type of accommodation you choose, the city offers excellent value for your baht. Scroll down to see our picks for some of the best hotels in Chiang Mai.
Tip: If you’re visiting during the hottest months (March, April and May), we recommend staying somewhere with air conditioning and ideally a pool as temperatures can soar to 40°C (104°F).

main_topic.h_title: Which is the best area to stay in Chiang Mai?
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: Chiang Mai is largely centred around the Old Town (adlink), and staying here is perfect for most tourists.
You can easily walk to most attractions, with temples and lots of restaurants just a short distance away. It’s one of the best places to stay in Chiang Mai for convenience.
For travellers researching where to stay in Chiang Mai, the Old Town is usually the first area worth considering thanks to its central location and historic atmosphere.
Another popular alternative is the Nimmanhaemin area, also known as Nimman (adlink), which has a lot of trendy cafés, boutique shops and a modern feel.
It appeals particularly to digital nomads and travellers who prefer a more contemporary neighbourhood while still being within easy reach of the main sights.
Staying just outside the city walls is also a great option, offering a chance to upgrade your accommodation or save a bit of money.
If you stay further from the city centre, be prepared to either have your own transport or rely on taxis and other forms of transport to get around.

main_topic.h_title: Yi’s Garden Villa
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: When we visited Chiang Mai, we stayed for 10 nights at Yi’s Garden Villa in the northeast part of the old town on a quiet road.

For an incredibly fair price, we got a large room with a sofa, table and a private balcony offering a panoramic view of the city and the mountains. Upon arrival, we initially stayed one night in one of the more “ordinary” rooms, which was also very nice.
The garden pool is big, and we enjoyed both swimming in it and dining beside it (where the lovely receptionist was kind enough to play with our baby from time to time).
Overall, the service level was much higher than the price we paid, and we had a wonderful stay.

primary_content.text: If you’re looking for an upgrade from Yi’s Garden Villa, U Chiang Mai is another great place.
The hotel offers a shared pool and a prime location in the old town, right on the main street where the Sunday Night Market takes place.
The rooms are decorated in calming tones, each with a small balcony. Guests can also make use of a (small) fitness room, and breakfast is a mix of buffet and à la carte options.

main_topic.h_title: The Inside House
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: If you’re looking for a private pool and a location within Old Town, and want to avoid paying a fortune, the 4-star hotel The Inside House is well worth considering.
The hotel draws on 1920s-inspired Lanna Colonial design, and some of the rooms and suites even have private marbled pools.
Breakfast is served à la carte, and daily afternoon tea is included in the rate – both get enthusiastic reviews.

Wat Phra Singh is a five-minute walk away, and Wat Chedi Luang is similarly close, so it’s one of the best places to stay in Chiang Mai if you want a convenient base for temple-hopping in the old town.

main_topic.h_title: Sireeampan Boutique Resort & Spa
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: Sireeampan, designed to resemble a Thai temple, is in fact a beautifully crafted boutique hotel located just north of the trendy Nimman area northwest of Chiang Mai’s old town.
It’s an intimate place to stay with only 11 rooms (each named after a precious gemstone), and both couples and families seem to love it here.
It is worth noting that the resort sits a short drive from the old town rather than within it, so you’ll want to factor in taxis or a hire bike if you plan to spend a lot of time exploring on foot.

That said, there’s a full-service spa with aromatherapy and reflexology, a poolside bar, a library and a garden to keep you occupied if you’re happy to slow down and let Chiang Mai come to you rather than the other way around.

main_topic.h_title: 137 Pillars House
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: 137 Pillars House is situated just across the Ping River, only a few minutes’ drive from Old Town.
The distance is actually part of the appeal: close enough to explore easily, far enough to feel removed from the tourist bustle.
The hotel is built around a restored 19th-century teak house with a rich colonial heritage, and the name comes from the original structure, which sat on exactly 137 pillars.
The 30 suites each feature their own outdoor areas with daybeds and two of them come with private plunge pools.
The 25-metre lap pool is worth a mention of its own. It’s flanked by a 12-metre high wall covered in lush greenery. A gorgeous stay in Chiang Mai for sure!

main_topic.h_title: Four Seasons Resort Chiang Mai
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: The best hotel in Chiang Mai is located half an hour’s drive north of the city centre, among rice paddies and mist-covered mountains in the Mae Rim Valley.
Once you arrive, however, you may find it hard to leave.
Elegant pavilions and private pool villas blend traditional Lanna architecture with contemporary comfort, and the whole place feels more like a small village than a hotel.
Facilities are extensive. There’s a spa with yoga overlooking the rice fields, two grass tennis courts, and a cooking school where you can learn to make proper Northern Thai food.
You can also explore the Mae Rim Valley on mountain bikes, or simply do very little by the pool.
We’d love to spend a couple of days relaxing at this resort!

main_topic.h_title: Transport to and from Chiang Mai
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: Chiang Mai is located approximately 700 kilometres (435 miles) north of Bangkok.
The fastest way to travel between Thailand’s two largest cities is, unsurprisingly, by plane. It’s also possible to drive or take the train.

main_topic.h_title: By plane
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: From Bangkok, you can fly to Chiang Mai from both Suvarnabhumi Airport (BKK) and Don Mueang Airport (DMK). The flight takes about an hour and 15 minutes.
There are also flights to Chiang Mai from many other cities in Thailand, as well as major cities across Asia.

main_topic.h_title: By bus or car
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: Depending on when you drive in or out of always-busy Bangkok, the journey takes around 9 hours.
Night buses are also available on this route.

main_topic.h_title: By train
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: The train journey between Bangkok and Chiang Mai takes between 10 and 14 hours depending on which departure you choose.
The night train is likely more comfortable than the night bus.

We’ve previously taken the night train from Bangkok to Surat Thani, and although it was a bit bumpy, we still managed to get some sleep. Some of the night trains between Bangkok and Chiang Mai even look rather appealing.

main_topic.h_title: When to visit Chiang Mai
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: As in the rest of Thailand, Chiang Mai generally experiences three seasons:
The cold season (high season) : November to February.
The warm season (low season) : March to May.
Rainy season (low season) : June to October.
The best times to visit Thailand and what to expect – from the tropical islands to the northern hills

main_topic.h_title: The cold season (high season)
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: If you visit Chiang Mai (and the rest of Northern Thailand) between November and February, you can expect cool temperatures and dry weather.
Be sure to bring a sweater for the evening, as it can get a bit chilly.
In mid-January or early February, the air quality usually becomes hazy due to the burning season fires, which typically begin sometime in January.

main_topic.h_title: The warm season (low season)
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: Northern Thailand gets extremely hot from mid-March and April until the arrival of the rains around May.
During the hot season, temperatures can reach around 40°C (104°F) in the day and air pollution tends to be quite bad.
Therefore, it’s generally not recommended to visit Northern Thailand during this time if you can avoid it.
We visited Chiang Mai ourselves in mid-May when the hot season lasted a little longer than usual.
On several days, there was a heatwave with temperatures between 32-37°C (~ 90-99°F) in the shade, and nights when the temperature only dropped slightly.
On the plus side, accommodation prices were low and many attractions weren’t too crowded with tourists.

main_topic.h_title: Rainy season (low season)
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: It’s always difficult to say exactly when the rainy season begins – but once the rains arrive in April, May or June, it marks the end of the burning season and the extreme heat.
The smoke gradually disappears, the waterfalls start flowing again and it becomes much more comfortable to be outdoors.
On the other hand, some roads can be tricky to navigate – especially in more remote parts of Northern Thailand. Trekking can also get quite muddy.

main_topic.h_title: What is the best time of year to visit Chiang Mai?
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: The season and weather naturally influence when it’s a good idea to visit Chiang Mai.
The most pleasant time of year is also the most popular, namely the high season between November and February. Prices tend to be higher around Christmas and New Year.

Tip: The Loy Krathong and Yee Peng light festivals take place during the full moon of the 12th month of the Thai calendar, which usually falls in November. These festivals mark the end of the rainy season with lanterns illuminating the sky and water – a stunning (yet polluting) spectacle.

main_topic.h_title: When not to visit Chiang Mai
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: In terms of weather, we would not recommend late March, April and early May.
It’s not an ideal time to visit Northern Thailand – unless you want to experience Songkran (the Buddhist New Year). It’s celebrated in mid-April, and it turns into a massive, public water fight.
It’s also best to avoid the burning season. See below for more on that.

main_topic.h_title: Burning season
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: In Northern Thailand (including Chiang Mai, Chiang Rai and Pai), the air quality is heavily affected by the annual burning season. Fields and forest areas are burned to clear land for the next growing season, leading to severe air pollution.
The burning season typically lasts from mid-January to mid-April, though the timing varies each year.
Haze can appear as early as December (after the rainy season ends in November), but pollution worsens significantly from late February.
Air pollution peaks in March but conditions improve once the rains return, usually around April and the Songkran festival.
Breathing in the polluted air is neither healthy nor pleasant, so if you have flexibility in your travel plans, it is best to avoid Northern Thailand during this period.

main_topic.h_title: Our best tips for Chiang Mai
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: Be mindful of the season and weather. The timing of your visit to Chiang Mai makes a big difference. Avoid the burning season, and bring light rain gear if visiting during the rainy season.

Transportation with Grab or Bolt is often cheaper than the local taxis. It works just like Uber. Simply download both apps, compare prices for your route, and make sure you have data on your phone to use them.

The electrical outlets in Chiang Mai generally feature two round prongs, fitting both most European and Asian appliances, as well as the flat prongs of USA and Japan. The standard voltage is 220 volts.
How long to spend in Chiang Mai is difficult to say. You can see the main attractions in a few days or spend months as a digital nomad.

Dress respectfully at the temples. Make sure your shoulders and knees are covered in religious surroundings. If possible, bring a sarong, which you can quickly tie around your waist or drape over your shoulders. They can also often be rented very cheaply.

Wear good shoes. You will be walking a lot in Chiang Mai, so bring sneakers or comfortable sandals. Shoes that are easy to take on and off are useful if you plan to visit many temples, as they must always be removed before entering.

Book accommodation well in advance if you’re travelling during the high season (November to February). While there will always be rooms available, many of the best hotels in Chiang Mai get fully booked months ahead of time.

Wifi is widely available in hotels and cafes, and it’s usually very fast. If you need internet access elsewhere for services like Grab and Bolt, consider buying a local SIM card or eSIM with data. It’s affordable and easy to obtain. We’ve previously used Airalo (adlink) with great success.
The sun is strong. Remember your sun protection and stay in the shade during the hottest hours in the middle of the day.
Credit cards are accepted in most higher-end establishments, but cash is more commonly used in local restaurants, smaller shops and regular taxis/tuk-tuks.

ATMs and currency exchange spots are easy to find in Chiang Mai. It’s usually most cost-effective to withdraw money in baht, and to minimise extra fees, it’s a good idea to take out the maximum allowed amount at once.
With several first-class hospitals, clinics and dental practices in Chiang Mai, medical care is readily available if you need treatment or assistance during your stay.
Bring your own water bottle and refill it at cafés, restaurants and water dispensers around the city, where a litre of clean water costs just a single baht (or less).

main_topic.h_title: Sustainable travel tips
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: To travel as sustainably as possible, we recommend the following:
Book eco-friendly accommodation such as hotels with a sustainability focus or owned by locals.
Minimise the use of air conditioning and turn it off when you are not in the room.
Buy handmade souvenirs directly from the artist instead of mass-produced items in larger stores.
Respect local traditions and follow the temple dress code.
Eat as plant-based, local and organic as possible.
Bring your own drinking water in a refillable bottle.
Avoid disposable plastics as much as possible.
Sort your waste correctly and do not throw it on the ground.
Take only photos and leave only footprints. Avoid taking things from nature with you.
Respect the local wildlife.

main_topic.h_title: Is the old town the best place to stay in Chiang Mai?
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: For most visitors, yes. Staying within the walls of the old town (adlink) puts you within walking distance of temples, restaurants and the Sunday Night Market, which makes it one of the best places to stay in Chiang Mai if you don’t fancy relying on taxis or tuk-tuks every day.

main_topic.h_title: Should I stay in old town or Nimman?
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: Old Town (adlink) suits travellers who want temples, markets and sights right on their doorstep.

Nimman (adlink), just northwest of the old town, leans more towards trendy cafés, shopping and a younger, more modern feel. Both are good options – it really just depends on what kind of holiday you’re after.

main_topic.h_title: What’s the best area to stay in Chiang Mai for first-time visitors?
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: The old town, hands down. It’s compact, walkable and puts you near most of the city’s famous temples. It’s perfect for first-timers or shorter stays.

main_topic.h_title: Is it worth staying outside Chiang Mai’s city centre?
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: It can be, particularly if you want a quieter stay or a bit more luxury for your money.
Just be prepared to arrange your own transport, as you won’t have everything on foot the way you would in old town.

main_topic.h_title: Is Chiang Mai expensive to stay in?
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: Not really, no. Even some of our favourite hotels in Chiang Mai, like Yi’s Garden Villa (adlink), offer a pool, air conditioning and good service for a fraction of what you’d pay elsewhere in Southeast Asia.
Luxury options like 137 Pillars House or the Four Seasons (adlinks) exist too, of course, if you fancy treating yourself.

main_topic.h_title: Do I need a hotel with a pool in Chiang Mai?
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: If you’re visiting during the hot season (March to May), we’d say it’s close to essential, but that’s just a personal preference.
Temperatures can climb to 40°C, and a pool makes a huge difference to how comfortable your stay feels.

main_topic.h_title: How far in advance should I book a hotel in Chiang Mai?
main_topic.main_title: Where to Stay in Chiang Mai? Best Hotels in All Price Ranges
main_topic.author: Alex & Victoria

primary_content.text: If you’re travelling during high season (November to February), book well ahead.
Rooms are rarely impossible to find, but the best hotels in Chiang Mai do get snapped up months in advance.

primary_content.text: Thank you for reading our guide on where to stay in Chiang Mai.
What are your thoughts on Northern Thailand’s (unofficial) capital? Where would you choose to stay?
Hopefully, the guide has provided some inspiration for the best hotels in Chiang Mai.
Feel free to ask us anything in the comments if you haven’t been to the city yet. We are happy to help.
If you’ve already been there, it would be great to hear your best tips and tricks for accommodation or the best area to stay in Chiang Mai, if you have a favourite.
